groups.text: The ledger holds fifty accounts, one thousand cents each.
Transfers move money between them, so the total stays five zero zero zero zero.
A reader wants that total.
It walks the accounts in id order.
Lock one, read it, add it, move on.
It has passed account three.
Now a transfer moves three hundred cents from account forty to account three.
What total will the reader get?
It reads the rest, and gets four nine seven zero zero.
It saw account three before the money came, and account forty after it left.
Every read was locked, and no transfer broke the books.
The sum mixes two moments.
It is torn.
In one Java run of the lesson's demo, seven thousand two hundred forty-one of nine thousand four hundred fifty-six sums were torn.
The fix: readers stop adding.
They read one field, latest, which points to the last finished snapshot.
Reader A reads it now, and holds version one.
To build the next one, the ledger takes every lock, in the id order transfers use.
Now no transfer is half done.
A transfer that comes now waits, for microseconds.
It copies all fifty balances into a new record, with the total and a version number.
Once built, the record never changes.
Then one volatile write publishes it, and latest now points to version two.
Then the locks go, in reverse order, and the waiting transfer runs.
Reader A read latest just before that write.
What does it see?
All of version one.
Old, but whole.
Reader B comes after, and sees all of version two.
Old or new, never a mix.
A snapshot never changes, and the pointer moves in one write.
Here it is in Java and Kotlin: every lock in id order, an immutable record, one volatile write.
The rule. Build the whole snapshot while no transfer can run, then publish it with one volatile write.
Check yourself. A reader asks for the latest snapshot in the middle of a transfer from forty to three.
Can it get four nine seven zero zero?
No. Every snapshot was copied with no transfer half done.
It gets five zero zero zero zero, maybe from a slightly older version.
